body.text: In 1968 Australia had around 140 education researchers. That number has since multiplied at least ten, and probably twenty, times in academic education research alone. Hundreds, perhaps thousands, more are at work in education departments and agencies, sundry other state and federal bureaucracies, non-government offices, think tanks and consulting firms.

The largest of these categories of education researchers, the academics, contributed an impressive 3.5 per cent of global output in academic education research in 2020. But consider the other side of the equation, the 96.5 per cent, and we see a truly staggering figure of 233,000 outputs. Even more startling, that 2020 total is ten times the 1995 figure; the 2026 number is probably around half a million. John Hattie was famously able to digest around 800 meta-studies “relating to achievement” in his 2009 book, Visible Learning; those 800 meta-studies were in their turn digests of something like 50,000 studies. Undaunted, so many researchers have kept on keeping on researching in that one area that Hattie’s 2023 edition draws on 2100 meta-studies based on 130,000 studies.

Something else can be learned from that example: almost all of the world’s academic education research output is instantly available to just about every education researcher anywhere in the world. What’s more, much of it is usable, for research and other purposes, just about anywhere.

Some questions arise. How much of this output is actually needed? How much of the education research done in Australia is simply repeating work done elsewhere? How much is used, even by other researchers? According to a report of a study by University of Melbourne researcher Matt Pinnuck, half of Australian research outputs in 2020 — all research, that is, not just education research — were cited just once a year, on average, in the five years following, while a quarter garnered three or less than three citations or reads. Australian education research apparently does better than the average, but better enough to make any real difference?

Then there’s the question of cost: a May 2026 working paper provided by Pinnuck reports big variations in average cost per output both over time and by size of institution, ranging from well over half a millions dollars per each to just a fraction of that ($169,000). We can guess that education research is closer to the low end of the cost spectrum than the high, but even tens of thousands of dollars per output, given the huge volume, soon adds up. Is it worth it? To whom?

And there arises yet another question: what else could have been done with that time, money and intellectual effort? What is the opportunity cost? Since most Australian academic research on education is done by researchers who also teach teachers-to-be, the first question is whether research is taking more time (and attention) from that teaching than it should. Perhaps more of the intellectual effort now spent on research in the academy should be spent elsewhere — in or with schools, for example?

The Australian branch of the global education research industry has been in a more or less continuous state of self-examination ever since the unfavourable report card on universities’ research efforts handed down by the Excellence in Research for Australia exercise in 2010. There have been round tables, conferences, consultations, strategies, plans and reports, along with a number of articles in the Australian Educational Researcher. In none of these has the questions posed above, questions of need, use, cost and opportunity cost, been prominent. To the contrary, the present disposition of education research has been taken as a given, as has its continuation into the indefinite future.

Also taken as self-evident: academic education research has made a large and wholly positive contribution educational practice. “Australian education research has a long and proud history of driving innovation, outcomes that have benefited generations of Australians, and contributed to our international standing as a prosperous, democratic society of knowledge, invention and ideas,” runs the summary of a 2024 conference of education researchers, peak bodies, professional associations and representatives of national education agencies. No evidence for these claims is given or cited.

What follows runs against this grain. It is impressionistic, reflecting my observations from several angles, as a member of staff of a teachers college that became a College of Advanced Education, or CAE, before being absorbed into a university; as (briefly) an academic education researcher; as a ministerial staffer in Canberra; as co-founder and co-compiler of the Good Universities Guides; as a consultant and commentator; and as a user of education research throughout.

What is now called “education research” was brought to Australia in 1930 by Americans bearing gifts. The Carnegie Foundation used an offer of funding to line up the lords of the land of schooling, the heads of five of the six state education departments — Queensland was having none of this nonsense — behind the idea of setting up an Australian agency to conduct and encourage rigorous and useful empirical research. “Usefulness” would be defined by the education departments. “Rigour” would be as understood in the US by its “scientific” branch of Psychology (represented on the new body’s governing board by local professors of that discipline and its relatives). And this research would, like Mr Gradgrind, deal in facts and nothing but the facts: “I shall regard research as meaning recognising and defining a problem,” wrote the second director of that new body, the Australian Council for Education Research, or ACER, in the 1950s, “designing procedures to provide partial or complete answers to it; collecting information by those procedures; collating and analysing the information and interpreting its results; and checking and testing the interpretations to be certain of their validity and general soundness.”

The ACER and its kind of research led a precarious existence before prospering in the postwar years, gradually at first, then explosively. A boom in school and then tertiary enrolments pushed numbers of education researchers from the prewar handful to around 150 FTEs (full time equivalents) in the mid 1950s and well over 200 in 1970. From that point numbers climbed almost vertically, driven less by the needs or demands of a booming and increasingly tumultuous education system than by developments on the production side of the equation: teacher agitation for “professional” status and qualifications forced teacher education out of the old department-run teachers colleges into CAEs and then universities, a process completed by the reforms launched by federal minister John Dawkins in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

There was just one difference between a “university” and the humble teachers college, but it was a fundamental one: universities, unlike teachers colleges, did research. The distinction was insisted upon as a matter of course by the original six universities, passing themselves off as “research intensive” de novo despite the fact that many faculties harboured an Anglophile disdain for the Americans and their publish-or-perish mania. The new universities (Monash, 1961, the first of them) and the very new (RMIT and others, late 1980s and early 1990s), anxious to establish themselves as the real deal, were as insistent on research as the “old” institutions. Within a very few years that once-disdained Americanism, the PhD, was established as a non-negotiable ticket of entry for staff of the former teachers colleges and CAEs.

Such a sudden and substantial expansion in the reach and scale of the university way of doing things would have had a considerable impact even had it been the only change at work, but it wasn’t. With “Dawkins” came a form of accountability intended to shake up what was seen as the sheltered-workshop culture of the academy. Henceforth, everything would be rated — academics, academic units, institutions, scholarly journals, everything, and what’s more they would be rated in ways that encouraged ranking.

That wasn’t Dawkins’s invention of course; the same kind of thing was happening around the world. With the arrival of the internet soon after, Australian education research became a part of a global research industry and ranking system, with consequences including the following.

1. Education research became an industry, and an increasingly competitive and increasingly enclosed one. Vast numbers of academic sole traders were now selling their wares in a global marketplace, and selling mostly not to external users/consumers but to each other. The currency of sale and purchase was the citation, weighted according to the rank-order position of its source. “Accountability” anchored in the metrics of an autarchic economy rather than in end-use encouraged citation circles, product repackaging, multiple authorship, metastasising sub-fields, the proliferation of scholarly journals, and other gaming. To take just the last of these: Australian education’s first scholarly journal, the Australian Journal of Education (published by the ACER) appeared in 1957; there are now somewhere between forty and fifty titles.

2. The vastly increased scale of education research and its increasingly competitive culture have driven the development of a more elaborate and exploitative division of academic labour, often experienced as a loss of “collegiality” and “intellectual vibrancy” and, in the lower ranks particularly, a loss of security. Pervasive competitiveness appears to have been a driver of steep increases in total research output — often mis-labelled as an increase in “productivity” — in Australia, up by almost 600 per cent since the year 2000 according to reports of Pinnuck’s findings. It is at least possible that education’s share of the total has risen in Australia as it has elsewhere.

3. The status anxieties of a low-prestige discipline (and particularly of its new recruits) combined with the dominance of American social science and the intense American-led reaction against the “progressive” ideas of the 1960s and 1970s to push education research, including education research in Australia, to produce numerically expressed “hard” evidence (rock-hard in the case of “gold standard” randomised control trials, according to its practitioners). Technical quality is more esteemed than worthwhileness; “research” has increasingly come to mean “finding out,” contributing to the “evidence base” or “filling gaps in the literature” rather than thinking through or trying to make sense of the disparate findings of an unruly field. The PhD has become a training in tunnel vision.

4. In the minds of the founding fathers of Australian education research — they were, without exception, male — “research” would assist in the on-going development of schooling by informing those responsible for it, the state education departments. But from the outset, and with gathering speed in the postwar years, the leading research agency, the ACER, influenced teaching and learning directly through its testing program.

As the widespread hostility of the 1960s and 1970s to test-dominated schooling was quelled, and as research became an industry rather than an ancillary activity, the ambitions of researchers expanded, a development for which Hattie is a representative as well as an influential figure. In their introduction to the International Guide to Student Achievement (2012), Hattie and his co-editor Eric Anderman argued that just as the steady cumulation of scientifically established knowledge by medical research had driven out quack cures and folk remedies, so would steadily-cumulating evidence replace “staff-room war stories,” as Hattie once put it.

A succession of big books argued or implied that practice must follow where this evidence led: Rutter et al’s Fifteen Thousand Hours (1979); the Reagan administration’s What Works (1986); Hattie’s Visible Learning (2009); and the late-blooming Sweller et al’s Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design (1998).

5. Such utopian hopes for the development of an education research discipline were founded on a misconception: teachers do not administer treatments, schools are not hospitals and students are not patients. The knowledge generated by medical research is “scientific” in the commonplace sense of that term: not free of dispute and controversy, but relatively authoritative, and cumulative. Most of the knowledge generated by education research is neither; if and as it enters the realm of “practice” it enters into complicated relationships with other forms of knowledge, often inexplicit, unconsciously or intuitively deployed, often local and personal or otherwise “contextual, usually “values-laden.” In their complexity these interactions are beyond the chemical; there is no prospect of a chemistry-like science in the medium term at least.

The efforts of the Australian Education Research Organisation and others to “disseminate” fixed dollops of putatively authoritative “evidence” are sometimes constructive, mostly not. The intention is not to stimulate, engage, encourage or enliven but to drive “application” and “implementation.” Other forms of knowledge are discounted, even denigrated. As recent developments in the NSW and Victorian government school systems demonstrate, this is knowledge in the service of the crudest forms of power.

Much of the impetus for using research in schools has come from the researchers, not the schools; note, for example, that the authors of Strengthening a Research-rich Teaching Profession for Australia (2018) were the Australian Teacher Education Association, the Australian Council of Deans of Education and the Australian Association for Research in Education.

6. The rise and rise of the academic mode of production in education research has affected schooling, teachers and teaching in several ways. At the simplest level, it has created a new career pathway for teachers, draining intellectually interested and/or intellectually-capable teachers into a physically, institutionally and existentially remote realm, generally seen as “above” schools. With that went the hope that schools might become hotbeds of thinking-and-doing, which was replaced by a view of schools as outlets for research-endorsed, centrally distributed content to be delivered by teachers to students in a standardised way. The standing and attractions of the “teaching profession” have been correspondingly reduced. Most consequently, a research-authorised push for standardisation of teaching works directly against efforts to adapt “curriculum” to the progress, needs and interests of students.

As senior education researchers Lawrence Ingvarson and Trevor Gale pointed out in an early (2010) and valuable contribution to the discussion of education research and its future, education is a field of policy and practice as well as a field of study. One thrust of the remarks above is that academic research has misconstrued its relationship with practice twice over, first by its enclosure and self-absorption and then by its complicity in the reduction of schools and teachers to mere retailers.

To the extent that this observation is warranted, it suggests that the on-going conversation among academic education researchers about their work and its future should focus less on the product and its consumption and more on the relations by which different forms of education-related knowledge are produced. In the first place, that might mean doing more research with and for practitioners rather than about practice.

But perhaps the point should be taken further? Most academic education research is done by teacher educators. So long as both research and the teaching of teachers-to-be are based in universities they will compete for time, attention and prestige, and teaching will lose. If, as I’ve argued, the practice of teaching in schools is being diminished by university-based research — and taking into account also the gross over-production of academic research (bound to be accelerated by AI), the less-than appealing conditions of work for many academics, and how students become teachers — perhaps it is time to go back to the future? To invert the university-school relationship? To base teacher education in schools along with a significant fraction of education research and researchers? •
